Endoglin null embryos die from defects in endocardial cushion development, and Endoglin is not required for endothelial cell development or angiogenesis.

Endoglin, a TGF-beta super family receptor that is required for normal cardiovascular development in humans, is dispensable for normal angiogenesis and vascular patterning in the midgestational mouse embryo, but is essential for endocardial cell to mesenchymally transition during formation of endocardial cushions in the developing heart.

Endoglin null ES cells contribute widely to the endothelial lineage in chimeric mice, but are excluded from the endocardial lineage in the heart, and that Endoglin function is dispensable for endothelial cell differentiation in the early midgestation mouse, but is essential for endocardial cell fate specification.

Endoglin null ES cells can contribute to endothelial cell populations in the chimeric embryo, but not to endocardial cushion mesenchyme, which is a specialized endothelial cell population that contributes to the formation of the cardiac outflow tract.
Endoglin null embryos die in midgestation due to a failure in endocardial cushion development and that this defect is cell autonomous to the endocardium.

The main takeaway from our work is that
Endoglin null embryos die in embryonic development with defects in multiple tissues.
Endoglin null embryos have a defect in the endocardial cushion that is not due to an intrinsic defect of the endothelium but rather is a result of an abnormality in the endocardium.
Endoglin null mouse embryonic stem cells contribute to the formation of all endothelial cells in chimeric mouse embryos rescued from the early lethality of the null allele.
